case_studies.title: Toward Secure LLM Agents: Threat Surfaces, Attacks, Defenses, and Evaluation
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly moving from conversational interfaces to software components that plan, invoke tools, maintain memory, and act on external environments. This transition changes the nature of security risk. In agentic settings, failures are no longer limited to unsafe text generation. Untrusted content may redirect control flow, misuse tool privileges, corrupt persistent state, leak sensitive information, or trigger harmful external actions. At the same time, research on LLM agent security is expanding quickly but remains fragmented across attack families, defense
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of security risks in large language model agents, building a framework to identify and mitigate threats, and resulting in a better understanding of potential attacks and defenses. The researchers developed a comprehensive approach to evaluate LLM agent security. This affects IT work as LLM agents are increasingly used in software components and automation tools.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that uses large language models, here is what to do: review your current security measures, assess potential threat surfaces, and evaluate the implementation of defense mechanisms to mitigate risks. This flags a risk: if your org uses LLM agents, check for untrusted content and tool privileges immediately. Ensure your security protocols are up to date to prevent potential attacks.
case_studies.score_reasoning: High novelty and IT relevance due to the subject of secure LLM agents, high potential value within 90 days for IT engineers and consultants looking to improve the security of their infrastructure.

case_studies.title: Harness In-Context Operator Learning with Chain of Operators
case_studies.abstract: Neural operators approximate mappings between function spaces, but often generalize poorly to other operators and usually require fine-tuning or retraining. In-Context Operator Networks (ICON) addresses this issue by prompting the model with numerical context so that the model learns specific operators from prompts and adapt to different operators without fine-tuning. However, ICON may still fail to generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) operator tasks. Inpired by the success of harness engineering of Large Language models (LLMs), we introduce Chain of Operators (CHOP), a framework that harne
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of neural operators generalizing poorly to other operators by building a framework called Chain of Operators that allows models to learn specific operators from prompts and adapt to different operators without fine-tuning, resulting in improved generalization to out-of-distribution tasks. The researchers introduced a framework that harnesses the power of in-context operator learning. This is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novel and potentially impactful framework for operator learning. High potential for deployment in MLOps pipelines. Real-world applicability in edge cases where fine-tuning may not be feasible. Could be adopted in IT environments with complex workflows but currently scores 10 in VALUE_90_DAYS due to technical barrier of implementing such framework.

case_studies.title: Zero Touch Predictive Orchestration: Automating Time-Series Models for the Cloud-Edge Continuum
case_studies.abstract: The Cloud-Edge Continuum (CEC) enables latency-critical applications by distributing resources to the far edge, but its extreme volatility makes proactive Zero Touch Management via time-series forecasting essential. However, orchestrators face a severe "cold start" problem: newly discovered nodes lack the historical data required to train localized predictive models, while generalized models fail to capture unique hardware and microservice behaviors. To solve this, we propose a fully automated time-series prediction architecture driven by a novel data-mixing methodology. At the infrastructure
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of managing volatile cloud-edge resources by building an automated time-series prediction architecture, which resulted in improved proactive management of latency-critical applications. The researchers created a novel data-mixing methodology to overcome the 'cold start' problem in training predictive models. This innovation enables more efficient distribution of resources to the far edge.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud-edge infrastructure, here is what to do: review your current predictive modeling approach, consider integrating automated time-series forecasting, and assess the potential for improved resource distribution using this new methodology. This flags a risk: if your organization uses generalized predictive models, check for potential failures in capturing unique hardware and microservice behaviors immediately. Not directly applicable to non-cloud edge IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses a specific issue in the cloud-edge continuum, which is relevant to IT engineers working on infrastructure and automation. However, its applicability and value in the next 90 days are limited, so it scores low on value.

case_studies.title: $τ$-Rec: A Verifiable Benchmark for Agentic Recommender Systems
case_studies.abstract: As recommender systems transition toward agentic, multi-turn conversational interfaces, evaluation paradigms have struggled to keep pace. Current benchmarks often rely on "LLM-as-a-judge" evaluations, which introduce subjectivity, high costs and inconsistency. We present $τ$-Rec, a benchmark for agentic recommender systems that replaces subjective evaluation with verifiable rewards and a reveal-tagged elicitation (RTE) mechanism that controls how task constraints surface during dialogue. By testing agents against structured catalog predicates and employing a pass^k reliability metric, $τ$-Rec
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating agentic recommender systems by creating a verifiable benchmark called $τ$-Rec, which replaces subjective evaluation with objective rewards and a new dialogue mechanism. The result is a more consistent and cost-effective way to test these systems. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on improving the evaluation of recommender systems rather than cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.score_reasoning: While the paper introduces a novel benchmark for agentic recommender systems, its direct relevance to IT engineers is limited. However, its novelty and AI maturity scores are high due to its cutting-edge topic.

case_studies.title: System Report for CCL25-Eval Task 5: New Dataset and LoRA-Fine-Tuned Qwen2.5
case_studies.abstract: Recently, large language models (LLMs) have achieved promising progress in the fields of classical Chinese translation and the generation of classical poetry. However, domain-specific research on precise translation and affective-semantic understanding of classical poetry remains limited. The main challenge is that most studies treat the poetic appreciation task as a general-domain problem, neglecting the distinctive features of poetic appreciation, while high-quality and domain-specific datasets are extremely limited. To address this limitation, we decompose the task into three subtasks: term
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of precise translation and affective-semantic understanding of classical poetry by creating a new dataset and fine-tuning a language model. The authors built a domain-specific dataset and used it to fine-tune a large language model, resulting in improved performance on poetic appreciation tasks. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work

case_studies.title: ALIGNBEAM : Inference-Time Alignment Transfer via Cross-Vocabulary Logit Mixing
case_studies.abstract: Domain fine-tuning degrades the safety of large language models: fine-tuned specialists readily comply with harmful prompts framed in domain language. Existing inference-time defenses that mix logits from a safe anchor model require both models to share a vocabulary, which rules them out for the cross-family specialists where safety is most degraded. We present ALIGNBEAM, a training-free method that lifts this restriction by translating anchor logits into the target model's vocabulary token-by-token at each decoding step; a small LLM judge then selects the safest among K candidate continuation
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of large language models complying with harmful prompts after domain fine-tuning. The researchers built ALIGNBEAM, a method that translates anchor logits into the target model's vocabulary to improve safety. The result is a safer large language model that can resist harmful prompts.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on improving the safety of large language models rather than managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.score_reasoning: While the paper provides some novelty, its relevance to real IT infrastructure and value in 90 days are moderate.

case_studies.title: Substrate Asymmetry in User-Side Memory: A Diagnostic Framework
case_studies.abstract: User-side memory in LLMs is typically scored as a single "personalization" capability: given a user's history, is the output more user-aware? We show this aggregate metric hides opposite-direction failures. Memory factorises into at least three orthogonal axes -- behavioral consistency (style, voice), factual presence (recall facts in history), and factual absence (abstain when a fact is absent) -- and no single substrate wins all three. Comparing per-user gamma-LoRA (a small LoRA adapter trained on each user's history; gamma denotes per-user, not per-task) against BGE-large dense top-K retrie
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of understanding user-side memory in large language models by breaking it down into three key aspects, creating a diagnostic framework to evaluate these aspects, and finding that no single approach excels in all areas. They built a framework to diagnose and compare different user-side memory approaches, including a per-user gamma-LoRA adapter. The result shows that a single metric is not sufficient to evaluate user-side memory capabilities.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on the development and evaluation of large language models rather than cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty: 10 (factorisation of user-side memory into orthogonal axes is a new perspective) + 23 (IT relevance: LLMs are relevant to IT engineers, especially when discussing real-world deployment) = 33. Relevance is high because the paper directly affects how IT engineers work with LLMs. Value is relatively low because it's a theoretical concept rather than a practical solution or a direct call to action.
